918.title: Vatican II lived
918.hook: Mass in local languages, the priest facing the people, more of the Bible read aloud
918.howItsDone: Catholic parishes generally celebrate Mass in the local language with the priest facing the people and lay readers proclaiming the first readings; in some places the older Latin form is also celebrated with the bishop's permission.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Good Pope John, Angelo Roncalli, who wrote about peace to all people of good will. Your line was all people of goodwill.

Ask an older Catholic what Sunday Mass sounded like when they were small, and some will describe the same scene. The priest stood at an altar against the far wall, his back to the people, praying in Latin, much of it quietly. In the pews, some followed in a missal with the translation printed beside it; others prayed the rosary on their own. Then, within a few years, the same parish changed. The priest turned around. He said The Lord be with you in English, or Spanish, or Tagalog. Lay people walked up to read. Bishops in Rome had met and written documents. This is the council in the pews.
screen: `THE PRIEST'S BACK, THE LATIN.` → `ROSARIES IN THE PEWS.` → `THEN HE TURNED AROUND.`

segments.voice: The Second Vatican Council's document on the liturgy is known by its opening Latin words, Sacrosanctum Concilium. Here's what it changed, and what it didn't. First, the language. It allowed the Mass and the sacraments to be celebrated more widely in the people's own languages. Catholics sometimes hear Pentecost in that, when the crowd in Jerusalem was amazed because, in the Douay-Rheims, "every man heard them speak in his own tongue." Second, the Bible. It asks that the treasures of Scripture be opened up more richly, so more of the Bible is read aloud at Mass. Third, the people. It speaks of the faithful taking part fully and actively, not as silent spectators. So lay people began to read, to sing the responses, to bring up the gifts. Fourth, the surprises. The document doesn't actually tell priests to turn the altar around; that came in the reforms that followed. It doesn't abolish Latin either. It says Latin is to be kept, and gives Gregorian chant a place of honor. Catholics still differ about all this. Some love the reformed Mass in their own language. Some are drawn to the older Latin form and attend it where it's allowed. And for some, Vatican II isn't first a document at all. It's the Sunday the priest turned around.
screen: `THE PEOPLE'S OWN LANGUAGE.` · `MORE OF THE BIBLE, READ ALOUD.` · `TAKING PART, NOT WATCHING.` · `LATIN KEPT, ALTAR NOT ORDERED.` · then, large: `EVERY MAN HEARD THEM SPEAK IN HIS OWN TONGUE.`

segments.voice: Walk through a Mass you've been to, in your mind, or any church you've stood in: where the altar is, which way the priest faces, what language you hear, who walks up to read. Find one thing the council touched and one thing that stayed old, a hymn, a statue, a Latin word that survived. If you pray, pray for that parish as it is now; if not, simply hold the room in mind.
Sacrosanctum Concilium. The Second Vatican Council's document on the liturgy, which opened the Mass to people's own languages and asked the faithful to take part fully and actively.
Your line: the council in the pews. A document from Rome, felt first on a Sunday morning. Day nine hundred eighteen, done.

919.title: Paul VI (1963–1978)
919.hook: the pope who boarded planes to Jerusalem, India and New York, and told the United Nations no more war
919.howItsDone: Catholics keep the feast of Saint Paul VI, and the Holy See keeps a permanent observer at the United Nations, where later popes have also addressed the General Assembly.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Vatican II lived, and Sacrosanctum Concilium: the Sunday the priest turned around. Your line was the council in the pews.

A thin man in white walks to a podium in New York. Before him sit the representatives of the world's nations, in the hall of the United Nations General Assembly. He is the bishop of Rome, a long way from Rome. He came by plane. He has no army and no vote in this hall, and he tells them he has nothing to ask for himself. Then, speaking in French, he says the words this day is built on. No more war. War never again. His name was Giovanni Battista Montini. As pope he was called Paul the Sixth.
screen: `A MAN IN WHITE IN NEW YORK.` → `NO ARMY, NOTHING TO ASK.` → `NO MORE WAR.`

segments.voice: Paul the Sixth came right after Good Pope John, and he's easy to overlook. First, the finisher. John called the council; Paul was elected between its sessions, with much of its work still ahead, and he brought it to its close and began putting it into practice. The Mass in local languages from yesterday came in under him. Second, the traveler. He took the name of Paul, the apostle who crossed the sea again and again, and he got on airplanes: to Jerusalem, where he embraced the Orthodox patriarch Athenagoras, to India, to New York. Third, the speech. At the United Nations he called himself an expert in humanity, a man with long experience of human beings, and he begged the nations: no more war, war never again. If they wanted to be brothers, he told them, let the weapons fall from their hands. Catholics hear in this Isaiah's old promise, in the Douay-Rheims: "nation shall not lift up sword against nation, neither shall they be exercised any more to war." Fourth, the cost. His years weren't calm. Some of his teaching, especially his letter on marriage and birth control, was hard for some Catholics to accept, and it's still argued over. The Church has since named him a saint. What stays is a man without an army, standing in a hall of flags, asking the nations to put the weapons down.

segments.voice: Picture that hall, a country's name on each card, and then the people behind the cards: diplomats who haven't slept, translators in their booths, peacekeepers far from home, staff who feed refugees. Pick one of them and stay with that person a while. If you pray, pray for them, perhaps with Isaiah's line about swords; if not, wish them steady hands.
Paul the Sixth. The pope who finished the council, traveled by plane, and told the nations at the UN: no more war.
Your line: no more war. Words from a man with no army, spoken to the nations. That's day nine hundred nineteen.

920.title: Oscar Romero (1917–1980)
920.hook: an archbishop in El Salvador, shot while celebrating Mass, now honored as a saint
920.howItsDone: Catholics keep the feast of Saint Óscar Romero, and in El Salvador and elsewhere people gather where he died, at the hospital chapel in San Salvador, and at his tomb in the cathedral.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Paul the Sixth, a man in white before the nations. Your line was no more war.

Sunday morning in El Salvador, and in kitchens and market stalls, radios are tuned to the archdiocese's station. The archbishop is preaching from the cathedral, and he goes on a long time. He explains the readings. Then he does something sermons don't usually do: he reads the news of the week. The names of people killed. People taken from their homes and not seen again. A village where soldiers came. He reads them out so that they will be heard by someone. The man at the microphone was Óscar Romero.
screen: `RADIOS ON A SUNDAY.` → `A SERMON THAT READS THE NEWS.` → `THE NAMES, READ ALOUD.`

segments.voice: Romero's story turns four times. First, the quiet bishop. When he was made archbishop of San Salvador he was known as a careful, bookish priest, and some expected him to keep his head down. Second, a friend's death. Soon after, his friend Rutilio Grande, a Jesuit priest who worked among poor farmers, was shot dead on a country road along with companions. Romero went to see the bodies and prayed over them that night. People who knew him say something changed in him there. Third, the voice. From then on his homilies, carried by radio, named what was happening to his people, and he said the Church had to be the voice of those who had no voice. A line in Proverbs sounds like his work, in the Douay-Rheims: "Open thy mouth for the dumb." Dumb there means those who cannot speak. In his last Sunday homily he turned to the soldiers themselves. They were farmers' sons too, he reminded them, killing their own brothers and sisters, and he asked them, in God's name, to stop. Fourth, the altar. The next day, as he finished his homily at Mass in the chapel of the hospital where he lived, a gunman shot him at the altar. The Church has since declared him a martyr and a saint, canonized alongside Paul the Sixth. He never ran for anything or carried a weapon. He read the Gospel on Sunday, and then he read out the names.
screen: `A CAREFUL, BOOKISH ARCHBISHOP.` · `A FRIEND KILLED ON A COUNTRY ROAD.` · `THE RADIO HOMILIES NAME THE DEAD.` · `SHOT AT THE ALTAR, NOW A SAINT.` · then, large: `OPEN THY MOUTH FOR THE DUMB.`

segments.voice: Let someone come to mind whose story doesn't get told: a worker at the edge of your town, a neighbor who doesn't speak the language, someone in a place the news has forgotten. Say their situation to yourself in one plain sentence, the way Romero read the names. If you pray, you can pray for them by name.
Oscar Romero. The archbishop of San Salvador who named his people's dead on the radio and was shot at the altar.
Your line: the voice of the voiceless. He lent his voice to names no one else would read. Until tomorrow.

921.title: The four churchwomen (1980)
921.hook: Maura Clarke, Ita Ford, Dorothy Kazel and Jean Donovan, killed in El Salvador
921.howItsDone: Maryknoll, the Ursulines of Cleveland and parishes in El Salvador and the United States remember the four churchwomen with Masses and vigils, especially on the anniversary of their deaths.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Óscar Romero, who read the names of the dead on Sunday radio. Your line was the voice of the voiceless.

Two of them have just flown back from a meeting in Nicaragua. The other two have driven out after dark to meet them at the airport outside San Salvador, in a white van. Four American women: two Maryknoll sisters, an Ursuline sister and a young lay volunteer. They know the roads, the checkpoints, the risk. The van never reaches home. Days later, local people point the way to a shallow grave by a country road. Their names were Maura Clarke, Ita Ford, Dorothy Kazel and Jean Donovan.
screen: `A VAN LEAVES THE AIRPORT.` → `FOUR WOMEN, ONE ROAD.` → `IT NEVER REACHES HOME.`

segments.voice: It would be easy to tell this as a story about how they died. Their lives say more. First, who they were. Maura Clarke and Ita Ford were Maryknoll sisters, members of an American Catholic missionary order. Dorothy Kazel was an Ursuline sister from Cleveland. Jean Donovan wasn't a nun at all: she was a lay missionary, a young woman with a business career behind her, who had come to help. Second, what they did. In a country at war, they drove refugees to safety, brought food and medicine to families hiding from the fighting, and helped bury the dead. Ordinary work, in a place where ordinary work had become dangerous. Third, the choice to stay. Friends and family asked them to come home. Jean Donovan wrote that she had thought about leaving, but couldn't bring herself to abandon the children she cared for. They knew what had happened to Romero. They stayed with the poor. Fourth, the truth told. Members of El Salvador's National Guard were later convicted of the killings, and questions about who gave the orders went on for years. Their families kept asking. Some Catholics read their story beside the Last Supper in John's Gospel, where Jesus says he will no longer call his disciples servants, and then, in the Douay-Rheims: "But I have called you friends." They hadn't gone to El Salvador to die. They went to be with people, and when staying became dangerous, they kept being with them.
screen: `THREE SISTERS AND A VOLUNTEER.` · `REFUGEES, FOOD, BURIALS.` · `ASKED TO LEAVE, THEY STAYED.` · `THE KILLERS CONVICTED, QUESTIONS REMAIN.` · then, large: `BUT I HAVE CALLED YOU FRIENDS.`

segments.voice: Picture someone far from home tonight because they chose to be with people who need help: a sister in a clinic, a volunteer at a border, a lay worker in a refugee camp, a doctor in a war zone. Think what their day might hold, a long drive, a checkpoint, a child who needs medicine. If you pray, pray for missionaries and the people they stay with; if not, wish them safe roads.
Jean Donovan. The lay missionary among the four churchwomen killed in El Salvador, who wrote that she couldn't bring herself to abandon the children she cared for.
Your line: they stayed with the poor. Asked to come home, they chose to stay. Day nine hundred twenty-one.

922.title: The Missionaries of Charity (1950)
922.hook: the sisters in white and blue saris, begun by Teresa of Calcutta, who care for the dying
922.howItsDone: Missionaries of Charity sisters, in their white saris with blue borders, run homes for the dying, the abandoned and the sick in many countries, and volunteers of any faith or none can often come to help with the daily washing, feeding and cleaning.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the four churchwomen, among them Jean Donovan, who were asked to come home and stayed. Your line was they stayed with the poor.

A long room in Kolkata, beside a Hindu temple. Rows of low beds, each holding someone found on the street, too sick to walk. A sister in a white sari with blue stripes kneels at one of them with a basin of water, washing a man's feet. He may not live through the week, and she knows it. She isn't there to cure him. She's there so that he doesn't die alone, unwashed, unnamed. The house is called Nirmal Hriday. The sisters are the Missionaries of Charity.
screen: `A LONG ROOM IN KOLKATA.` → `A SISTER WITH A BASIN.` → `SO NO ONE DIES ALONE.`

segments.voice: The order was begun by the woman Catholics now call Saint Teresa of Calcutta, Mother Teresa, a teacher who left her convent school to live among the city's poorest people. Start with the promise. Like other sisters, they make vows of poverty, chastity and obedience, and their rule adds one more: wholehearted and free service to the poorest of the poor. Free means no payment, ever. Then the thirst. In their chapels, beside the crucifix, the sisters put two words from the cross in John's Gospel, in the Douay-Rheims: "I thirst." They hear in them Jesus thirsting for love, and they see him in the person on the bed. Then the work, which grew far beyond Kolkata: homes for the dying, for abandoned children, for people with leprosy or AIDS, soup kitchens in big Western cities. There are brothers and priests in the same family now too. The work is plain: washing, feeding, sitting, holding a hand. And the questions. Not everyone has praised it. Some critics, including doctors who visited, questioned the standard of medical care in the homes. Supporters answer that the homes were meant for comfort and presence at the end, not hospital treatment. Both are part of the honest story. Today's line comes from a British journalist who filmed the sisters and called his book Something Beautiful for God, after a phrase tradition links with Mother Teresa. Not something impressive. Something beautiful, like a clean bed and a held hand.
screen: `A TEACHER LEAVES HER SCHOOL.` · `FREE SERVICE TO THE POOREST.` · `I THIRST, BESIDE THE CROSS.` · `PRAISED, AND QUESTIONED.` · then, large: `I THIRST.`

segments.voice: Hold in mind someone who is dying or very ill: a grandparent, a friend in a hospice, a stranger in a hospital you passed. Picture their room and someone sitting with them, and ask, gently, whether that someone could ever be you. If you pray, pray for them and for all who care for the dying; if not, simply hold them in mind.

Your line: something beautiful. Small and plain, for someone who can't repay it. See you soon.

923.title: John Paul II (1978–2005)
923.hook: a pope from Poland who opened his papacy crying be not afraid
923.howItsDone: Catholics keep the feast of Saint John Paul II, and his words be not afraid are often sung, printed on banners, and quoted at confirmations and youth gatherings.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Missionaries of Charity at Nirmal Hriday: a basin of water and a held hand. Your line was something beautiful.

Saint Peter's Square, packed. The new pope stands before the crowd at the Mass that begins his papacy: broad-shouldered, a former actor with a voice that carries. He comes from a country behind the Iron Curtain, under a communist government wary of the Church. Partway through his homily he says it, then says it again: be not afraid. Open wide the doors for Christ. Open the borders of states, of economic and political systems. Do not be afraid. His name was Karol Wojtyła. He took the name John Paul.
screen: `A NEW POPE, A FULL SQUARE.` → `FROM BEHIND THE IRON CURTAIN.` → `BE NOT AFRAID.`

segments.voice: Those words weren't a slogan dreamed up on the day. They came out of a life. Loss came first. Karol grew up in a small Polish town, and by the time he was a young man his mother, his only brother and his father had all died. Then the occupation. When Nazi Germany occupied Poland, the universities were shut. He worked in a stone quarry and a chemical plant, acted in an underground theater that performed in people's living rooms, and studied for the priesthood in a secret seminary. Any of it could have cost him his life. Then the long middle. As priest and then archbishop of Kraków, under a communist government, he hiked and skied and kayaked with students, taught philosophy, and pushed for churches the state didn't want built. So when he said be not afraid, he spoke as someone who had been afraid with good reason, and had gone on anyway. The words belong to the Gospels first. When the disciples see Jesus walking toward them on the water at night and cry out in terror, he says, in the Douay-Rheims: "Be of good heart: it is I, fear ye not." John Paul's papacy was long and sometimes argued over, and the coming days look at a few of its moments. But the opening note was this one: the fear is real, and the voice on the water speaks to it anyway.
screen: `A CHILDHOOD OF LOSS.` · `QUARRY, SECRET THEATER, SECRET SEMINARY.` · `A PRIEST UNDER COMMUNISM.` · `THE WORDS COME FROM THE WATER.` · then, large: `BE OF GOOD HEART: IT IS I, FEAR YE NOT.`

segments.voice: Let one thing come to mind that you've been putting off because it scares you: a conversation, an apology, a doctor's appointment, saying no, saying yes. Notice where the fear sits in your body, breathe there, and shrink the brave thing down to its first small step. If you pray, pray the line from the water: be of good heart, fear ye not.
Secret seminary. Where Karol Wojtyła studied for the priesthood in secret during the Nazi occupation of Poland, before he became Pope John Paul the Second and said be not afraid.
Your line: be not afraid. A man who knew loss and danger said it first to a full square. Rest well.

924.title: Solidarity
924.hook: John Paul II's visits home to Poland and a peaceful workers' movement that changed the country
924.howItsDone: In Gdańsk, a monument to the shipyard workers stands at the gate where the strike began, and Polish Catholics visit the grave of Blessed Jerzy Popiełuszko at his Warsaw parish.

segments.voice: Yesterday, John Paul the Second, the pope from Poland. Your line was be not afraid.

A gate at a shipyard on the Baltic coast of Poland. The workers inside are on strike, locked in. On the gate hang flowers, a picture of the Virgin Mary, and a photograph of the Polish pope. Outside, families pass food through the bars. Inside, a priest hears confessions in the open yard, and the strikers kneel on the concrete for Mass. The strike leader is an electrician with a big mustache named Lech Wałęsa. The movement being born on that dock will be called Solidarity.
screen: `A SHIPYARD GATE ON THE BALTIC.` → `FLOWERS, MARY, THE POPE.` → `MASS ON THE CONCRETE.`

segments.voice: First, the visit. Not long after he became pope, John Paul went home to Poland, then under a communist government. Enormous crowds came out. In Warsaw he prayed aloud that the Spirit would come down and renew the face of the earth, and then added: the face of this land. He was borrowing a psalm, in the Douay-Rheims: "thou shalt renew the face of the earth." Some who were there say people looked around and realized how many of them there were. Second, the strike. At the shipyard in Gdańsk, workers struck, and out of the strikes came Solidarity, a trade union the government didn't control. Its badge became the word itself, painted in tumbling red letters. Third, the hard years. The government declared martial law, banned the union and jailed its leaders. Solidarity went underground. A young Warsaw priest, Jerzy Popiełuszko, held Masses for the country and preached a line from Saint Paul, in the Douay-Rheims: "overcome evil by good." The secret police murdered him. His funeral became a sea of people, and still the movement didn't turn to violence. Fourth, the end. The government sat down with Solidarity at a round table and agreed to partly free elections, and Solidarity's candidates swept the seats open to them. Communist rule in Poland ended without a civil war, and some historians link the movement to the wider changes that soon followed across Eastern Europe. Catholic teaching calls solidarity a virtue: a firm commitment to the good of every person, because we are all responsible for all. In Poland, it was also a union card.
screen: `THE POPE GOES HOME.` · `A STRIKE BECOMES A UNION.` · `MARTIAL LAW, A MARTYRED PRIEST.` · `A ROUND TABLE, NOT A WAR.` · then, large: `OVERCOME EVIL BY GOOD.`

segments.voice: Count the people who worked yesterday so your life could run: whoever picked your food, drove the truck, cleaned the building, stocked the shelf. Pick one face and wonder what their shift is like, and what would make it fairer. If you pray, pray for workers with Paul's line, overcome evil by good; if not, hold them with gratitude.
Solidarity. The Polish workers' union born in the Gdańsk shipyard, and a Catholic virtue: a firm commitment to the good of all.
Your line: without violence. The week ran from Vatican II through Paul the Sixth, Romero, the four churchwomen, the Missionaries of Charity and John Paul, to Solidarity. That's the week.
